Connections and curvature from symmetries of an algebra

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), September 2026, at Ultra. Not yet reviewed. Public domain (CC0).

An action of a Lie group supplies directions in which elements of an algebra can be differentiated. A finite projective module plays the role of a vector bundle. A connection differentiates its sections, and curvature measures the failure of successive derivatives to agree with the Lie bracket. An invariant trace turns powers of this curvature into ordinary Lie algebra cohomology classes.

We assume a unital complex C*-algebra , a finite-dimensional real Lie group , and an action continuous in norm on each element. We also use matrix functional calculus and finite projective modules. The convention for a right-module inner product is , linear in the second argument. Basic references are [Khalkhali 2007] and [Connes 1980]. The lesson Cyclic cohomology: traces, differentials and symmetry explains the graded-trace mechanism that will appear below.

Theorem 6.1. The smooth algebra consists exactly of series

whose coefficients decrease faster than every power of . The coefficient defines the unique normalized trace on .

Proof. Fourier projection for the torus action is

Laurent polynomials in are dense by the definition of the generated C*-algebra. On them this projection has range . Continuity and the fact that this one-dimensional space is closed give the same range on . If is smooth, integration by parts in both torus variables bounds its coefficient after multiplication by arbitrary powers of . Equivalently, applying powers of gives arbitrary powers of . Thus the coefficients are rapidly decreasing.

Conversely, a rapidly decreasing series and every series obtained by multiplying its coefficients by a polynomial in converge absolutely in norm, since the monomials are unitaries. Termwise differentiation of the orbit series is justified uniformly on the torus. It gives all derivatives and proves smoothness. Fourier uniqueness follows, for example, by convolving the orbit function with product Fejér kernels, which converge in norm to its value at the identity.

The torus average is a positive unital map with scalar range; let . The monomial multiplication rule is

Both orders have zero scalar coefficient unless ; in that case both phases equal . Thus is a trace on polynomials and, by norm continuity, on . For any normalized trace, invariance under conjugation by and forces its value on each nonconstant monomial to be zero, because is irrational. Density proves uniqueness.

(c) Take . Then , and the displayed defect sends both off-diagonal units to their negatives. Since , the defect is not the identity and is not a group action. Pointwise inner implementation alone does not make the two-by-two family an action: the cocycle law must hold coherently in both parameters. Here 's scalar defect is central, but is not central in , so it survives on the off-diagonal entries.

For the two-parameter version set and ; restriction to the first coordinate gives exactly the same failure. The example shows why these chosen pointwise implementers cannot be used in the matrix proof. It does not refute Theorem 5.1: the genuine cocycle implements the same trivial diagonal actions and gives a valid matrix action.

[Rieffel 1988] Marc A. Rieffel, Projective modules over higher-dimensional non-commutative tori, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 40 (1988), 257–338. Author-hosted paper. The finite-frame method above is a direct two-dimensional realization of the Schwartz-space construction of projective modules.

[Pimsner–Voiculescu 1980] Mihai Pimsner and Dan Voiculescu, Exact sequences for K-groups and Ext-groups of certain cross-product C*-algebras, Journal of Operator Theory 4 (1980), 93–118. Journal-hosted paper.

[Blackadar 1998] Bruce Blackadar, K-Theory for Operator Algebras, second edition, Cambridge University Press (1998). Author-hosted book.

[Connes 1982, §13, first lemma, p. 39] Alain Connes, A survey of foliations and operator algebras, author-posted edition. Author-hosted survey. Proposition 1.3 supplies the full smooth-replacement and exterior-equivalent fixed-projection conclusion in a coefficient-cocycle convention.
